title: Rules for discernment
hook: learning to read the movements of the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, three kinds of people: one puts it off, one bargains, one wants only what serves God. Your line was really free. Where did you catch yourself bargaining? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-seven.

A wounded soldier is stuck in bed, bored, in a house with the wrong books: no adventure stories, only a life of Christ and lives of the saints. So he alternates. For hours he daydreams about a great lady and glorious deeds. Then he reads, and daydreams about doing what the saints did. Both daydreams are pleasant while they last. But afterward, as Ignatius tells it later, he notices something odd. The knightly dreams leave him dry and unsatisfied. The saintly ones leave him content, long after the book is closed. He starts paying attention to the aftertaste. That habit grows into a set of rules. Today's word.
screen: `A SOLDIER IN BED, WITH THE WRONG BOOKS.` → `TWO KINDS OF DAYDREAM.` → `HE NOTICES THE AFTERTASTE.`

segments.voice: In everyday speech, discernment means good taste or sound judgment. Ignatius means something narrower. His Rules for the Discernment of Spirits are about the movements inside a person: the pulls, moods and thoughts that come and go in prayer and in ordinary days. He names the two big ones. Consolation is any movement that draws a person toward God: more faith, hope and love, a quiet peace, even tears. Desolation is the reverse: darkness, restlessness, a drag toward low things, feeling as if far from God. The subtle part follows. The same feeling can mean opposite things, depending on which way a person is heading. For someone drifting away from God, the enemy offers easy pleasures, and the good spirit stings the conscience. For someone growing toward God, it flips: now the enemy is the one who stings and discourages, and the good spirit gives courage and peace. So a feeling isn't a verdict. It's a signal, read in context. The First Letter of John says something like it, in the Douay-Rheims: "believe not every spirit, but try the spirits if they be of God." Try, as in test. One plain, practical rule: in a time of desolation, make no change. Stay with what you decided in a clearer hour. And in consolation, store up strength for the next dark stretch. He adds that the enemy behaves like someone who wants a secret kept, and loses power once things are told to a wise confessor or guide. Outside prayer this is quietly useful. The urge to quit everything at eleven at night may not be the voice to trust.
screen: `CONSOLATION AND DESOLATION.` · `THE SAME FEELING, TWO MEANINGS.` · `IN DESOLATION, MAKE NO CHANGE.` · `TELL IT TO A WISE GUIDE.` · then, large: `TRY THE SPIRITS IF THEY BE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice today's movements. Settle, and breathe. Let today replay quickly, like flipping through photos on a phone. Stop at one moment that left a good aftertaste: lighter, warmer, more open. Then stop at one that left you dry, tight, restless. Don't analyze them yet. Just name them: this one drew me toward. This one pulled me away. Notice where in the body each one sits. If you pray, you can bring both to God and ask for light to read them. The bell holds the time.
Discernment. For Ignatius, learning to read the movements of the heart, consolation and desolation, and where each one leads. Today's word.
Your line: read the heart. Today, when a strong mood hits, before acting on it, ask one question: which way is this pulling me? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: People who pray in the Ignatian way use the rules for discernment of spirits throughout a retreat and in daily life, often talking over their consolations and desolations with a spiritual director.

fork.setup: you're in a dark, restless stretch, and you want to drop a commitment you made in a peaceful time. what do Ignatius's rules say?
options: drop it now, while you feel it so clearly.
hold steady: make no change in desolation.
make some other big decision to feel better.
fork.reveal: in desolation, make no change; stay firm in what you decided before. the dark stretch is the wrong time to redraw the map.

original.note: Greek: a sorting, a telling apart. Paul names the discerning of spirits among the gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:10.

notes: The rules are paraphrased: rules 1–2 (the flip by direction of life), 3–4 (consolation and desolation), 5 (make no change in desolation), 10 (in consolation, prepare for desolation), 13 (the enemy wants secrecy, like a false lover). Confirm.

The convalescence story (books of chivalry wanted, only a life of Christ and lives of saints available; worldly daydreams leaving him dry, holy ones leaving him content) follows the Autobiography, ch. 1, in paraphrase; the 'great lady' is from the same passage. Confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording of 1 John 4:1; Greek 'διάκρισις' (1 Cor 12:10 has the plural διακρίσεις πνευμάτων). Confirm.
